\chapter{The Words Behind Please and Sorry}
\label{ch:favor-y-culpa}
\hlchaptermodality{320}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the favour, the trouble, the shame, the luck and the fault behind a Spanish courtesy.}

Complete ES-C320-culpa: open por favor into el favor, answer thanks with no es molestia, and place a fault with es mi culpa.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el favor]{el favor — the word you have been saying for a long time}

\label{lesson:ES-C320-favor}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{another book}, then \emph{a little water}. (\emph{\textbf{Otro}} libro; \emph{\textbf{poca}} agua.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item por favor — this word is already inside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fa-VOR}, the stress on the second beat. The \emph{v} is soft, closer to a \emph{b} made without closing the lips. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el favor} — \textquotedblleft{}a favour,\textquotedblright{} a good turn done for somebody.

Latin \textbf{favēre} meant \emph{to be well disposed toward} — to be on someone's side. The noun \textbf{favor} was what that goodwill looked like when it did something.

You have been carrying it without opening it. \emph{\textbf{Por favor}} is \emph{por} plus \emph{favor}: \textbf{for a favour}. Every time you have said \emph{please} in Spanish you have been saying \emph{as a good turn to me}. Now the second half stands on its own: \emph{un favor} is a thing you ask for, and \emph{el favor} is the one being asked.

English has it three ways over: a \textbf{favour} is the good turn, your \textbf{favourite} is what your goodwill lands on, and \textbf{favourable} weather is weather on your side.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five courtesy words that name what politeness is actually made of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el favor}
  \item \emph{un favor, por favor}
  \item \emph{otro favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{favēre} mean? (To be well disposed toward somebody.) And what is hiding inside \emph{por favor}? (\emph{Favor} — a good turn.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la molestia]{la molestia — the weight you are asked to carry}

\label{lesson:ES-C320-molestia}



\begin{quote}
What is the second half of \emph{por favor}? (\emph{Favor}.) And what does \emph{poco} measure? (A little of something.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mo-LES-tia}, the stress in the middle. The \emph{s} and \emph{t} run together with no vowel between them. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la molestia} — \textquotedblleft{}the trouble,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the bother.\textquotedblright{}

Underneath it is Latin \textbf{mōlēs}: a mass, a heavy bulk, the word Romans used for a breakwater or a great pile of stone. Something \textbf{molestus} was something with that weight on it. \textbf{Molestia} is the weight itself.

So a bother in Spanish is not an irritation. It is a load — a thing somebody has to carry for you. That is why \emph{no es molestia}, \textquotedblleft{}it is no trouble,\textquotedblright{} is the warm answer to thanks: you are saying \emph{nothing was carried}.

English kept the mass and shrank it. A \textbf{molecule} is \emph{mōlēs} with a little-ending on the end: a tiny mass. The pile of stone and the smallest piece of matter are the same Latin word at two sizes.

\emph{Molestia} ends in \emph{-a} and takes \emph{la}, like \emph{la casa} and \emph{la mesa}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The word that lets you tell somebody they cost you nothing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la molestia}
  \item \emph{no es molestia}
  \item \emph{un favor — no es molestia}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{mōlēs}? (A heavy mass, a pile of stone.) Which English word is that same mass made tiny? (\emph{Molecule}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la pena]{la pena — the price a feeling costs}

\label{lesson:ES-C320-pena}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a favour}, then \emph{it is no trouble}. (\emph{Un favor}; \emph{no es molestia}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PE-na}, two beats, stress on the first. A plain \emph{n}, not the \emph{ñ}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la pena} — \textquotedblleft{}sorrow,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}a shame,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}a penalty.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{poena} was a price: the payment a wrongdoer owed. Greek lent it to Latin, where it had meant the blood-price paid to a dead man's family. It has been about paying from the beginning.

Spanish kept both ends. \emph{La pena} is still the legal penalty, and it is also the ache — because sorrow is what a loss costs you.

English took it three separate times. \textbf{Pain} came the long way through French and softened into feeling. \textbf{Penal} and \textbf{penalty} came straight off the Latin and stayed legal. And a \textbf{subpoena} is \emph{sub poena}, \emph{under penalty}: a summons that names the price of not coming.

\emph{¡Qué pena!} — \textquotedblleft{}what a shame\textquotedblright{} — is the everyday one. You will hear it for a cancelled plan and for a real grief, and the word does not change size.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One word that reaches from a courtroom to a friend's bad news.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la pena}
  \item \emph{¡Qué pena!}
  \item \emph{no es molestia — es una pena}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{poena} mean first? (A price paid, a penalty.) What does \emph{sub poena} mean, word for word? (Under penalty.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la suerte]{la suerte — the token you drew}

\label{lesson:ES-C320-suerte}



\begin{quote}
What is a \emph{molestia}? (A trouble, a weight carried.) And what did \emph{poena} mean before it meant sorrow? (A penalty, a price.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SUER-te}. The \emph{ue} is one gliding sound, as in \emph{bueno}, and the \emph{r} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la suerte} — \textquotedblleft{}luck.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{sors}, and in its other form \textbf{sortem}, was a physical object: a marked token dropped into a jar and shaken out. Rome settled questions that way. Your \emph{sors} was the token that came out for you, and from there it became your lot, your share, your fate.

English built a surprising amount on that jar. To \textbf{sort} things is to put each into the pile its token names. A \textbf{sorcerer} is a \emph{sortiarius}, one who works by casting lots. Your \textbf{consort} is \emph{con} plus \emph{sors}: the person whose lot is drawn with yours. A soldier's \textbf{sortie} is a going-out on whatever lot fell.

The \emph{o} in \emph{sortem} broke into \emph{ue} on the way to Spanish, the same break that turns \emph{bueno} and \emph{puerta} out of \emph{bonus} and \emph{porta}.

\emph{¡Buena suerte!} is the wish. It agrees: \emph{buena}, because \emph{suerte} takes \emph{la}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A wish you can hand somebody at the door.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la suerte}
  \item \emph{¡buena suerte!}
  \item \emph{qué pena — buena suerte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{sors}, as an object? (A token drawn from a jar.) Why is it \emph{buena suerte} and not \emph{bueno}? (\emph{Suerte} takes \emph{la}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la culpa]{la culpa — five words for what politeness is made of}

\label{lesson:ES-C320-culpa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{what a shame}, then \emph{good luck}. (\emph{¡Qué pena!}; \emph{¡buena suerte!})
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CUL-pa}. The \emph{c} is hard, as in \emph{cat}, and the \emph{u} is a full round vowel. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la culpa} — \textquotedblleft{}the fault,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the blame.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{culpa} meant exactly this, and it came into Spanish unchanged — five letters carried two thousand years without losing one.

English never quite translated it. \textbf{Mea culpa}, \emph{my fault}, is still said in Latin. A \textbf{culprit} is the one the fault attaches to. Something \textbf{culpable} is something the fault can be laid on, and to \textbf{exculpate} is to carry the fault back out of somebody.

Spanish does not say \emph{I am at fault}. It says \emph{la culpa es mía} — the fault is mine — or shorter, \emph{es mi culpa}. The fault is a thing that belongs to somebody, and you name whose. That is why the answer that clears a person is \emph{no es tu culpa}: not a denial of the trouble, a return of the object.

Set beside \emph{lo siento} and \emph{perdón}, which you already have: those two say what you feel and what you ask for. \emph{Culpa} says where the thing sits.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words that name the parts of courtesy: the good turn, the weight, the cost, the token drawn, and the fault. None of them is a phrase you repeat. Each one is a thing you can put in a sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la culpa}
  \item \emph{es mi culpa}
  \item \emph{no es tu culpa — buena suerte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Spanish say \emph{it is my fault}? (\emph{Es mi culpa} — the fault is mine.) Which English word is \emph{culpa} with a person attached? (\emph{Culprit}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
